source_refs.note: Exercise 4.2, Question 7: Find |AA^t| and |A^tA|, parts (i)-(ii) (book page 60).

blocks.explanation:
\(A\) is \(2 \times 3\), so \(A\) itself has no determinant; but \(AA^{t}\) (\(2 \times 2\)) and \(A^{t}A\) (\(3 \times 3\)) are square.
We must form both products and find their determinants.
Plan: write \(A^{t}\), multiply (row by column), then evaluate each determinant.
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
To find: \(|AA^{t}|\) and \(|A^{t}A|\).
Method: Transpose (rows become columns), matrix multiplication (entry = row of the first \(\cdot\) column of the second), then the determinant rules.

Write the transpose
\[A^{t} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Row 1 of \(A\) becomes column 1 of \(A^{t}\), row 2 becomes column 2. \(A^{t}\) is \(3 \times 2\).

Check
\[R_1 + R_2 = (9, 1, 10) = R_3\]
Why: One row is the sum of the other two, so \(R_3 - R_1 - R_2\) is a zero row: the determinant must be 0. (In general \(A^{t}A\) here is made from only two columns of length 2, so it cannot have a non-zero \(3 \times 3\) determinant.)

blocks.explanation:
Now \(A\) is \(3 \times 2\): \(AA^{t}\) is \(3 \times 3\) and \(A^{t}A\) is \(2 \times 2\).
Plan: write \(A^{t}\), form both products, evaluate the determinants.
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
To find: \(|AA^{t}|\) and \(|A^{t}A|\).
Method: Transpose, multiplication, determinants.

Write the transpose
\[A^{t} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Columns of \(A\) become rows of \(A^{t}\).

Find \(A^{t}A\) (\(2 \times 2\))
\[A^{t}A = \begin{bmatrix} 9+4+1 & 3+4+3 \\ 3+4+3 & 1+4+9 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 10 \\ 10 & 14 \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Entry \((i, j)\) = column \(i\) of \(A\) \(\cdot\) column \(j\) of \(A\).

Check
\[R_1 + R_3 = (16, 16, 16) = 2R_2\]
Why: In \(AA^{t}\), \(R_1 + R_3 - 2R_2\) is a zero row, so \(|AA^{t}| = 0\) as found.
